model.label: Tax-funded national health service run by the Health Service Executive: public hospital care is free to all residents, but free GP care depends on income or age (medical card, GP visit card), and nearly half the population buys community-rated private insurance, mainly for faster hospital access

overview.statement: Every resident of Ireland is entitled to publicly funded health services, in full or in part; how much is covered depends mainly on the person's income and age (2025 profile).

Ireland's national health service is funded mainly from general taxation, which paid for 77% of total health spending in 2023; the Department of Health sets policy and oversees performance, and the Health Service Executive (HSE) manages and delivers publicly funded health and social care.

The HSE runs its own hospitals and community services but also buys care from others: GPs, dentists, pharmacists, allied health professionals, state-funded voluntary hospitals, grant-aided community organisations, private hospitals and home care agencies.
Public hospital care became universal in 2023 after user charges for inpatient stays were abolished; medical cardholders get free primary care, but there is no universal entitlement to primary care.

financing.statement: In 2024 government schemes financed 78% of current health spending; voluntary schemes, mostly private health insurance, paid 12%, and households paid the remaining 10% directly out of pocket (CSO System of Health Accounts 2024).

locator.section: More than three-quarters of healthcare expenditure is financed by government

financing.statement: Most government health spending in 2024 was funded from general government revenue (that is, general taxation); social insurance contributions such as PRSI covered only about 1% of government health spending.

locator.section: Where do the Financing Schemes source their revenue?

financing.statement: Social insurance contributions financed €223 million of health spending in 2024: €152 million from employers, €61 million from employees and €11 million from the self-employed.

financing.statement: Voluntary private health insurance paid for 12% of total health spending in 2023, nearly three times the EU average of 5%, and this high uptake is the main reason Ireland's private share of health spending is above the EU average.
Insurers' total premium income from private health insurance reached €3.6 billion in 2024, according to the Health Insurance Authority.
The average premium paid by adult members of private health insurance plans was €1,740 as of 1 January 2025, up from €1,594 on 1 January 2024.
Community rating of private health insurance is supported by a stamp duty paid on each health insurance contract purchased.

The state subsidises private health insurance through tax relief at source: premiums are reduced by the standard income tax rate (20%) applied to no more than €1,000 of premium per adult and €500 per child, for policies providing medical cover (Revenue guidance, reviewed May 2026).
The 2025 government budget allocated €24.3 billion to health, 6% more than the year before.
Health took 23% of total government expenditure in 2023, the largest share of any EU country (EU average about 15%).

covered.statement: According to the 2025 profile, some 14% of people qualified for a GP visit card giving free GP care to a wider group, including all children under 8, adults aged 70 and over, and people aged 8-69 below certain income thresholds.
GPs act as gatekeepers to secondary care; they are mostly private practitioners paid mainly through public schemes, with some income from patients' fees.

Public funding covers 79% of retail pharmaceutical spending, far above the EU average of 59%, because HSE reimbursement schemes (the Drugs Payment Scheme, the Long-Term Illness Scheme and medical cards) make medicines free or capped for those eligible (2025 profile).
Public funds covered only 78% of spending on hospital care in 2023, well below the EU average of 91%.

Several services have recently been made free at the point of use, among them contraception for people aged 17-35, fertility treatment, specialist menopause clinics and hormone replacement therapy (2025 profile).
The Department of Health has begun a long-term review of eligibility and entitlement rules, focused on primary and community care.

cost_sharing.statement: Over half of the population (57%) has neither a medical card nor a GP visit card and pays out of pocket for GP and allied health consultations, at €55-75 per visit, among the highest fees in the EU (2025 profile).

Medical cardholders get medicines for a small prescription charge, and the Drugs Payment Scheme caps any household's spending on medicines at €80 a month; together with insurance top-ups, households paid only 21% of retail medicine spending in 2023, the third-lowest share in the EU (EU average 36%).
Out-of-pocket payments were 11% of health spending, below the EU average of 16% (2025 profile).
Nearly 30% of household out-of-pocket spending goes on long-term care and 20% on medicines (EU average for medicines: 26%).
In 2016, community-dwelling adults in the Irish Longitudinal Study on Ageing (TILDA) spent a median €144 a year out of pocket on prescription medicines (interquartile range €0-€312).

additional_care.statement: 46% of the population held voluntary private health insurance in 2024, mainly to get faster access to hospital care and to cover part of their out-of-pocket costs.

Voluntary private health insurance mainly acts as supplementary cover for getting around access barriers rather than full coverage: policies typically give faster access to hospital specialists and private beds, and partly refund services the public system covers little, such as dental care and routine GP visits.

The price of private health insurance depends on the services and treatments covered, not on the buyer's medical history, past claims or age, and open enrolment guarantees the right to buy any plan on the market.

Four commercial insurers sell inpatient private health insurance to the public (Irish Life Health, Laya Healthcare, Level Health and Vhi Healthcare); restricted membership undertakings insure only their own members.
2.52 million people had private health insurance at the end of 2024, 1.3% more than a year earlier; the regulator thinks the slowing growth may be due to cost.
In 2024, 68% of people with private health insurance had a plan with restricted cover for joint replacement (75% of under-65s, 36% of those aged 65 and over).
Private insurers' payouts are shifting to private hospitals: in 2024 private hospital treatment made up 49% of claims paid, while public hospitals' share fell to 13% from 15% in 2023.

access.statement: In 2024, 5% of adults in Ireland who needed medical care said their need went unmet because of cost, travel distance or waiting times, above the EU average of 3.6%.
In a 2024 Eurofound survey, 5% of adults in Ireland reported unmet need for primary care (EU average 3%) and 6% for mental health care (EU average 7%).
Although GP numbers have risen substantially in recent years, they are unevenly spread, with GP density varying twofold between counties.
The number of people on outpatient waiting lists fell by just over 4% between September 2021 and September 2025, mostly because far fewer people were waiting more than one year or 18 months.
The Waiting List Action Plan, launched in late 2021, targeted long waits and set a goal that 90% of outpatients would wait under 12 months by the end of 2025.
Long outpatient waits cluster in four high-volume specialties: in dermatology, ophthalmology, neurology and endocrinology, one patient in five or more has waited longer than a year (2025 profile).
Waiting times for cataract, hip and knee surgery have not improved substantially since 2019; in 2024 just over half of patients waited longer than the 12-week Sláintecare benchmark.

Long waits for elective care have given households a reason to buy private health insurance for faster access in private facilities, so timely treatment is often influenced by the ability to pay privately, through insurance or out of pocket.

Ireland had 2.9 hospital beds per 1,000 people in 2023, against an EU average of 5.1, and curative bed occupancy has routinely been above 80% (except in 2020), compared with an EU average of 68% in 2023.

According to the 2024 EFPIA Patients W.A.I.T. Indicator, centrally authorised medicines took on average 645 days from EU marketing authorisation to reach patients in Ireland in 2024, and by mid-2024 only 31% of medicines approved by the European Commission in 2020-2023 were available in Ireland.

outcomes.statement: Life expectancy at birth was 82.9 years in 2023, more than a year above the EU average and the eighth highest in the EU.
The age-standardised avoidable mortality rate was 203 per 100,000 people in 2022, 21% below the EU average of 258.
Treatable mortality from stroke was 4.5 per 100,000, about half the EU average of 9.2 (2025 profile).

In 2023, 5.6 of every 100 people admitted for a heart attack died within 30 days, 9% fewer than the EU average of 6.1; 30-day mortality after ischaemic stroke fell 32% between 2013 and 2023, the second largest fall in the EU.
Five-year cancer survival for 2019-2022 was 66% for colorectal cancer (up 3 percentage points), 25% for lung cancer (up 7), 88% for breast cancer (up 4) and 65% for cervical cancer (up 4).
Avoidable hospital admissions for COPD and asthma were nearly double the EU average in 2023, while admissions for congestive heart failure were 39% below it and diabetes admissions in line with it.

Breast and cervical cancer screening participation was 15-20 percentage points above the EU average in 2023; colorectal screening reached 48%, in line with the EU average but below the national target of 50%.
Measles vaccination coverage fell from 92.3% in 2018 to 89.7% in 2024.
In the GBD 2019 study, Ireland's Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index score for ages 0-74 was 90.1 (95% uncertainty interval 88.0-91.5) in 2019, 19.7 points higher than in 1990.

costs.statement: Health spending was €36.3 billion in 2024, up 9.1% on 2023; that equals 11.3% of modified gross national income (GNI*), compared with an OECD average of 9.3% of GDP.
Health spending was 6.5% of GDP in 2024 (OECD average 9.3%), but measured against modified gross national income (GNI*), which removes globalisation effects, it was 11.3%.
Preliminary estimates put total health spending at €38.8 billion in 2025, 7% more than in 2024.
Health spending per person was €4,474 in 2023 (adjusted for purchasing power), nearly 17% above the EU average of €3,832.
Inpatient care took 35% of health spending in 2023 (EU 28%) and long-term care 22% (EU 18%).
Pharmaceuticals and medical devices took 12% of health spending in 2023, well below the EU average of 18%.
Under its pricing Framework Agreement with the pharmaceutical industry, Ireland obtained a 9% rebate on exclusive patented medicines; the agreement was due for renegotiation in 2025.

what_works.statement: Stroke care performs close to its targets: in 2023, 11% of stroke patients received thrombolysis (target 12%), 11% received thrombectomy, and the median door-to-needle time of 53 minutes beat the 60-minute goal.
The profile credits Ireland's National Cancer Control Programme, including concentrating cancer services in eight designated high-volume centres, with contributing to better cancer outcomes.
Pharmaceutical spending was 7% below the EU average in 2023, and cost-containment measures are estimated to have saved about €1.6 billion since 2013.

Among community-dwelling adults in the Irish Longitudinal Study on Ageing (TILDA) in 2016 who had any out-of-pocket prescription costs, having fewer healthcare entitlements was associated with 4.74 times higher out-of-pocket prescription spending (95% CI 4.37-5.15); the authors say this shows the benefit of expanding entitlements and making sure eligible people take them up.
The Sláintecare Implementation Progress Report 2024 reported that 95% of GPs had signed up to the Chronic Disease Management Programme.
The public health workforce doubled, from about 250 full-time equivalents in 2019 to about 500 in 2024.

problems.statement: With so little spare bed capacity, hospitals are exposed to predictable seasonal surges, leading to recurring winter overcrowding and postponed elective care.
Physician density was 3.8 per 1,000 people, below the EU average of 4.3 (2025 profile), and over 40% of doctors in Ireland in 2024 had trained abroad.
Only 37% of doctors who finished specialty training in 2023 took up posts in Ireland.
The HSE's 2022 recruitment freeze made existing staff retention problems worse and sped up emigration, according to the 2025 profile.

The large gap between the share of people insured privately (46%) and the share of spending private insurance actually funds (12%) raises value-for-money concerns and reflects long public waiting times that keep demand for insurance high.

A study of the creation of regional health structures in 2018-2023 found weak accountability arrangements, poor transparency, and periods of unclear roles and responsibilities for key decisions in the reform.

A study of Ireland's COVID-19 hospital access policy found that ending the agreement with private hospitals was heavily influenced by private hospital consultants, revealing strained relations with, and misunderstanding of, the private sector.
The Health Insurance Authority's 2023 consumer survey found affordability to be the main reason people do not have, or drop, private health insurance.

reforms.statement: Six HSE Health Regions, each with its own budget to plan and deliver services for its population, were set up in 2024; from March 2025, 20 Integrated Healthcare Areas began rolling out in five of the six regions.
Two 2023 measures widened public cover: inpatient hospital charges were abolished and free primary care was extended to children up to age 8, with a government commitment to extend it to age 12.
A new public-only consultant contract pays hospital specialists more if they work only in the public sector, including evenings and weekends; by May 2025, 64% of hospital consultants had taken it up.
The Sláintecare 2025+ report sets out system-wide reform programmes for 2025-2027 and beyond; the current government is the third to support Sláintecare, first published in 2017.
The plan sets out 23 programmes under three priorities: better access to health and social care, better service quality, and more capacity.
Between 2020 and 2024, 1,218 additional inpatient hospital beds were commissioned.
To ease doctor shortages, some tasks such as prescribing for common conditions have been opened to advanced nurse practitioners and pharmacists.
Integrated primary and community-based programmes for chronic disease were introduced step by step: type 2 diabetes in 2018, COPD and asthma in 2020, and congestive heart failure in 2021.
A Health System Performance Assessment framework launched in June 2023 tracks outcomes, access, quality and equity with 268 indicators across five dimensions.
In March 2020 the state made a Safety Net Agreement with 19 private hospitals, which the authors describe as the first time Ireland had universal, single-tier access to hospital care.
